blocks.body:
A small bakery makes trays of bread and trays of cake. Each tray of either kind spends one hour in the oven, and the oven is free for $4$ hours. A tray of bread needs $1$ hour of a baker's time and a tray of cake needs $3$, and the baker has $6$ hours. A tray of bread earns a profit of $2$ and a tray of cake a profit of $3$. How many of each should be made?

Problems with a linear goal and linear limits are called linear programs (program means plan, not computer code). We solve small ones by drawing, see why the answer is at a corner and how the simplex method finds it in large problems, and use duality to prove that an answer is optimal. You need [[solving-inequalities]] and a little of [[linear-systems]].

blocks.title: Writing down the problem
blocks.body:
Let $x$ be the number of trays of bread and $y$ the number of trays of cake (we allow fractions; think of them as average daily amounts). The problem is:
$$\text{maximise } 2x + 3y \quad\text{subject to}\quad x + y \le 4,\quad x + 3y \le 6,\quad x \ge 0,\quad y \ge 0.$$

The ingredients are decision variables ($x$, $y$), a linear objective to maximise or minimise, and linear constraints. A point satisfying all constraints is called feasible, and the set of all feasible points is the feasible region. It may be empty (the constraints contradict each other), and the objective may be unbounded on it (it can be made as large as we like). Otherwise there is an optimal solution.

blocks.title: Solving by drawing
blocks.body:
With two variables we can draw. Each inequality is a half-plane: $x + y \le 4$ is everything on or below the line $x + y = 4$, and $x + 3y \le 6$ is everything on or below the line through $(6, 0)$ and $(0, 2)$. Together with $x, y \ge 0$, the feasible region is the quadrilateral with corners
$$(0,0),\quad (4, 0),\quad (3, 1),\quad (0, 2).$$
The corner $(3,1)$ is where the two lines cross: subtracting $x + y = 4$ from $x + 3y = 6$ gives $2y = 2$.

Now picture the objective. The points where $2x + 3y = k$ form a line, and changing $k$ slides it parallel to itself. Start with a small $k$ and slide the line upward as far as it can go while still touching the region. The last point it touches is a corner. Checking the corners:
$$2\cdot 0 + 3\cdot 0 = 0,\quad 2\cdot 4 + 0 = 8,\quad 2\cdot 3 + 3\cdot 1 = 9,\quad 0 + 3\cdot 2 = 6.$$
The best plan is $3$ trays of bread and $1$ of cake, with profit $9$.

blocks.title: The corner principle
blocks.body: If the feasible region of a linear program in two variables is a nonempty bounded polygon, then the objective attains its maximum (and its minimum) at a corner of the polygon. The same holds in any number of variables, with corners of a bounded polyhedron, called vertices.

blocks.title: Proof in two variables
blocks.body:
First look at a single segment from $P$ to $Q$. Its points are $P + t(Q - P)$ for $0 \le t \le 1$, and a linear objective $f$ takes the values $f(P) + t\,(f(Q) - f(P))$ there, which change steadily with $t$. So on a segment, $f$ is largest at one of the two endpoints.

The feasible region is an intersection of half-planes, so it is convex: the segment between two of its points stays inside it. Take any feasible point $R$. Draw any line through $R$; because the region is bounded, the part of the line inside the region is a segment whose two endpoints lie on the boundary. By the first paragraph, $f(R)$ is at most $f$ at one of these endpoints, call it $S$. Now $S$ lies on an edge of the polygon, which is itself a segment between two corners, so $f(S)$ is at most $f$ at one of these corners. Hence $f(R) \le f(\text{some corner})$ for every feasible $R$, and the largest of the finitely many corner values is the maximum. The minimum is handled the same way.

blocks.title: The simplex method
blocks.body:
With $50$ variables and $100$ constraints a polyhedron can have astronomically many vertices, so checking them all is hopeless. Dantzig's simplex method (1947) walks from vertex to vertex along edges, each time improving the objective, and stops when no edge leads uphill.

Here is the walk for the bakery. Start at $(0,0)$, profit $0$. Cake earns more per tray, so increase $y$ while keeping $x = 0$. The oven allows $y \le 4$, but the baker allows only $y \le 2$, so we stop at the vertex $(0,2)$, profit $6$. Now move along the baker's line $x + 3y = 6$, increasing $x$. On this line $y = (6 - x)/3$, so the profit is $2x + (6 - x) = x + 6$, which increases with $x$. We continue until the oven constraint $x + y \le 4$ blocks us, at $(3, 1)$, profit $9$. From $(3,1)$ both edges lead downhill: along the oven line the profit is $2x + 3(4 - x) = 12 - x$, falling toward $(4,0)$, and going back along the baker's line lowers $x + 6$. So $(3,1)$ is optimal.

On a computer the walk is done with row operations as in Gaussian elimination, after adding a slack variable to each constraint (for example $x + y + s_1 = 4$, $s_1 \ge 0$, where $s_1$ is unused oven time). The simplex method is very fast in practice, although Klee and Minty (1972) built deformed cubes in $n$ dimensions on which Dantzig's original pivoting rule visits all $2^n$ vertices; the ellipsoid method (Khachiyan, 1979) and interior-point methods (Karmarkar, 1984) are provably fast in the worst case.

blocks.title: Duality: proving that an answer is optimal
blocks.body:
How could the bakery convince a sceptic that $9$ is truly the best, without the picture? Add the constraints with suitable multipliers. Take $\frac32$ of the oven constraint and $\frac12$ of the baker constraint:
$$\tfrac32(x + y) + \tfrac12(x + 3y) = 2x + 3y \le \tfrac32\cdot 4 + \tfrac12\cdot 6 = 9.$$
So no feasible plan beats $9$, and $(3,1)$ achieves it. The multipliers are a certificate of optimality.

Which multipliers work? For any $u, v \ge 0$ we have $u(x + y) + v(x + 3y) \le 4u + 6v$. The left side is $(u + v)x + (u + 3v)y$, and it is at least $2x + 3y$ whenever $u + v \ge 2$ and $u + 3v \ge 3$ (because $x, y \ge 0$). The best bound comes from a new linear program, the dual:
$$\text{minimise } 4u + 6v \quad\text{subject to}\quad u + v \ge 2,\quad u + 3v \ge 3,\quad u, v \ge 0.$$
Its optimum is $u = \frac32$, $v = \frac12$ with value $9$: the same number as the original problem.

The dual has a meaning. Someone wants to rent the oven and the baker, paying $u$ per oven hour and $v$ per baker hour. The bakery agrees only if the hours used for one tray earn at least as much rented out as baked, which is exactly the dual's constraints; the renter wants to pay as little as possible. The optimal values $u = \frac32$, $v = \frac12$ are called shadow prices: one extra oven hour would raise the best profit by $\frac32$ (from $9$ to $10.5$), and one extra baker hour by $\frac12$, as long as the same two constraints stay the binding ones.

blocks.title: Weak and strong duality
blocks.body:
Let $A$ be an $m \times n$ matrix, $b \in \mathbb{R}^m$, $c \in \mathbb{R}^n$. The primal problem is to maximise $c^{\mathsf T}x$ subject to $Ax \le b$, $x \ge 0$, and the dual problem is to minimise $b^{\mathsf T}y$ subject to $A^{\mathsf T}y \ge c$, $y \ge 0$ (inequalities between vectors hold entry by entry).

1. Weak duality: if $x$ is primal feasible and $y$ is dual feasible, then $c^{\mathsf T}x \le b^{\mathsf T}y$.
2. Strong duality (stated here without proof): if the primal has an optimal solution, so does the dual, and the two optimal values are equal.

blocks.title: Proof of weak duality
blocks.body:
Since $x \ge 0$ and $A^{\mathsf T}y \ge c$ entry by entry, $c^{\mathsf T}x \le (A^{\mathsf T}y)^{\mathsf T}x = y^{\mathsf T}(Ax)$. Since $y \ge 0$ and $Ax \le b$, $y^{\mathsf T}(Ax) \le y^{\mathsf T}b$. Together, $c^{\mathsf T}x \le b^{\mathsf T}y$.

Strong duality is deeper; its standard proofs go through the simplex method or through a separation theorem for convex sets (Farkas' lemma), and we do not give one here. A useful consequence of the two parts together is complementary slackness: at optimal $x$ and $y$, every constraint that is not tight has dual price $0$, and every positive dual price belongs to a tight constraint. For instance, if the bakery's oven had $10$ free hours, the best plan would be $6$ trays of bread (profit $12$) with $4$ oven hours unused, and the oven's shadow price drops to $0$.

blocks.title: Example 1: a cheapest diet
blocks.body: Food A costs $3$ per portion and gives $1$ unit of protein and $3$ units of vitamins. Food B costs $4$ per portion and gives $2$ units of protein and $1$ unit of vitamins. We need at least $4$ units of protein and $6$ of vitamins. Find the cheapest combination.
blocks.solution:
With $x$ portions of A and $y$ of B: minimise $3x + 4y$ subject to $x + 2y \ge 4$, $3x + y \ge 6$, $x, y \ge 0$.

The feasible region lies above both lines and is unbounded, but costs are positive, so a minimum exists. Its corners are $(0, 6)$ on the $y$-axis, $(4, 0)$ on the $x$-axis, and the crossing of the two lines: from $3x + y = 6$ we get $y = 6 - 3x$, and then $x + 12 - 6x = 4$ gives $x = \frac85$, $y = \frac65$.

Costs: $(0,6)$ gives $24$, $(4,0)$ gives $12$, and $\left(\frac85, \frac65\right)$ gives $\frac{24}{5} + \frac{24}{5} = \frac{48}{5} = 9.6$. The cheapest diet is $1.6$ portions of A and $1.2$ of B.

The corner principle was stated for bounded regions, so we should check that nothing further out is cheaper. Here a certificate does it: adding $\frac95$ times the protein constraint and $\frac25$ times the vitamin constraint gives $3x + 4y \ge \frac{36}{5} + \frac{12}{5} = \frac{48}{5}$ for every feasible point.

blocks.title: Example 2: shipping at least cost
blocks.body: Bakery A has $30$ crates and bakery B has $20$. Shop P needs $25$ crates and shop Q needs $25$. The cost per crate is $4$ from A to P, $6$ from A to Q, $5$ from B to P and $3$ from B to Q. How should the crates be shipped?
blocks.solution:
Let $a$ be the number of crates from A to P. Then everything else is forced: A sends $30 - a$ to Q, P needs $25 - a$ more from B, and Q needs $25 - (30 - a) = a - 5$ from B. All four amounts must be at least $0$, which gives $5 \le a \le 25$.

The total cost is
$$4a + 6(30 - a) + 5(25 - a) + 3(a - 5) = 290 - 4a,$$
which is smallest when $a$ is largest. So $a = 25$: A sends $25$ to P and $5$ to Q, B sends $20$ to Q and none to P, for a cost of $100 + 30 + 60 = 190$.

This is a transportation problem. The supply and demand equations left one free variable, so the feasible region was a segment and the optimum sat at an end. When supplies and demands are whole numbers, the vertices of a transportation problem always have whole-number coordinates, so solving it as a linear program never splits a crate.

blocks.title: Example 3: a bound by adding inequalities
blocks.body: Nonnegative numbers $x, y, z$ satisfy $x + y \le 3$, $y + z \le 4$ and $z + x \le 5$. Find the largest possible value of $x + y + z$, and of $x + y + 2z$.
blocks.solution:
Adding all three constraints gives $2(x + y + z) \le 12$, so $x + y + z \le 6$. Equality needs all three constraints tight: $x + y = 3$, $y + z = 4$, $z + x = 5$, which gives $x = 2$, $y = 1$, $z = 3$, all nonnegative. So the maximum is $6$, and the dual multipliers are $\left(\frac12, \frac12, \frac12\right)$.

For $x + y + 2z$, add the second and third constraints: $x + y + 2z \le 9$. Equality needs $y + z = 4$ and $z + x = 5$, so $x = 5 - z$ and $y = 4 - z$; the first constraint becomes $9 - 2z \le 3$, so $z \ge 3$, and $y \ge 0$ needs $z \le 4$. Every $z$ in $[3, 4]$ works, for example $(2, 1, 3)$ and $(1, 0, 4)$, both giving $9$. The maximum is $9$, attained along a whole edge of the feasible polyhedron between two vertices. This is allowed by the corner principle: the maximum is attained at a vertex, but perhaps not only there.

blocks.body:
- Checking only the corners is valid only when an optimum exists. If the region is unbounded the objective may have no maximum at all; if the region is empty there is nothing to optimise.
- Rounding a fractional optimum to whole numbers can give an infeasible or far from optimal plan. Problems that require integer answers (integer programming) are much harder in general: the decision version is NP-complete.
- Not every crossing of two constraint lines is a corner: $x + 3y = 6$ meets $y = 0$ at $(6, 0)$, which violates $x + y \le 4$. Always check feasibility.
- A shadow price is valid only for small changes. Increase the oven time enough and a different pair of constraints becomes binding, and the price changes.

Linear programming is the simplest case of [[convex-optimisation]], where duality carries over and interior-point methods are the main algorithms; its multipliers are the inequality version of [[lagrange-multipliers]]. Maximum flow and minimum cut in [[network-flows]] are a dual pair of linear programs, and so are maximum matching and minimum vertex cover in bipartite graphs (see [[cycles-matchings]]). The feasible regions are convex sets, the subject of [[convexity]]. Von Neumann's minimax theorem for two-player zero-sum games is equivalent to linear programming duality. On the computational side, see [[algorithms]] and the discussion of integer programming in [[p-vs-np]].

1. Maximise $x + 2y$ subject to $x + y \le 5$, $y \le 3$, $2x + y \le 8$, $x, y \ge 0$, and find multipliers that prove your answer optimal.
2. Write down the dual of: maximise $5x + 4y$ subject to $2x + y \le 8$, $x + 2y \le 7$, $x, y \ge 0$. Solve both problems and check that the optimal values agree.
3. Show that the constraints $x + y \ge 5$, $x \le 2$, $y \le 2$ have no solution, by adding suitable multiples of them to reach a contradiction.
4. For the bakery, find the profit per tray of cake at which the best plan changes from $(3, 1)$ to $(0, 2)$.
